PAPER: Original Article JHSMR Journal of Health Science and Medical Research Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Properties of the Thai Version of the Modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale in Individuals with Long COVID Guntee Thititriratana, M.Sc., Premtip Thaveeratitham, Ph.D., Thaniya Klinsophon, Ph.D. Department of Physical Therapy, Faculty of Allied Health Sciences, Chulalongkorn University, Pathum Wan, Bangkok 10330, Thailand. Received 5 September 2024 l Revised 25 February 2025 l Accepted 4 March 2025 l Published online 3 July 2025 Abstract: Objective: To translate and cross-culturally adapt the modified coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRSm) into a Thai version, and assess its psychometric properties in individuals with long COVID. Material and Methods: The C19-YRSm underwent translation and cross-cultural adaptation to produce a Thai version. Its 2 subscales, symptom severity and functional ability, were examined using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). In instances where the results were deemed unfit, alternative factor structures were explored through exploratory factor analysis (EFA). After that, internal consistency and test-retest reliability were calculated at 2-day intervals. Construct validity was assessed by examining correlations between the Thai version of the 36-item Short Form Health Survey questionnaire (Thai SF-36) and the Thai Fall Efficacy Scale-International (Thai FES-I). Results: The study sample comprised 338 individuals with long COVID. The results of the CFA indicated a poor fit. Subsequent evaluation using EFA revealed that the symptom severity and functional ability subscales were rearranged into 3 new subscales: major symptoms, minor symptoms, and functional ability. Internal consistency was found to be good to excellent (Cronbach’s alpha: 0.77-0.90). Test-retest reliability for all subscales of the Thai C19-YRSm demonstrated high consistency (intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC ): 0.88-0.95). Convergent validity showed moderate to strong (2,1) correlations with the Thai SF-36, while discriminant validity, compared to the FES-I, showed fair to poor correlations. Conclusion: The vigorous psychometric properties of the questionnaire make it highly suitable for cross-cultural research, enabling the assessment of long COVID severity among Thai individuals in clinical and research settings. JSON: Name: thai_c19yrsm_psychometrics Title: Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale in Thai adults with long COVID using confirmatory and exploratory factor analysis Short Hypothesis: Cross-cultural adaptation of the modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale into Thai will produce an instrument with a three-factor structure (major symptoms, minor symptoms, functional ability) and psychometric properties meeting prespecified thresholds (Cronbach's alpha ≥ 0.70 per subscale and ICC(2,1) ≥ 0.75 for test-retest) in Thai adults with long COVID. Related Work: Existing instruments for long COVID symptom assessment include the original C19-YRS and the modified C19-YRSm, developed with Rasch methods and previously reported to show strong internal consistency and acceptable subscale intercorrelations under a two-factor model (symptom severity and functional ability). Psychometric reports on the C19-YRSm indicate good internal reliability and moderate-to-strong test-retest ICCs in original-language samples, and prior studies used confirmatory factor analysis to support a two-factor structure. However, cross-cultural performance has not been established for many non-English settings. Comparators for construct validity commonly include generic health-status measures (SF-36) and domain-specific scales (FES-I); Thai translations for these comparators exist and show adequate reliability. Limitations in prior work include reliance on single-language samples, limited cross-cultural adaptation evidence, potential model misspecification when transferring factor structures across cultures, and sparse assessment of responsiveness and alternative factor solutions (e.g., EFA or Rasch re-calibration) in translated versions. Abstract: This research pipeline details the cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the modified COVID-19 Yorkshire Rehabilitation Scale (C19-YRSm) translated into Thai to assess long COVID symptom severity and functional impact. We will perform forward-backward translation, expert review, and cognitive pretesting, then administer the Thai C19-YRSm to a large sample of Thai adults with long COVID. We will test the original two-factor model via confirmatory factor analysis (CFA); if model fit is inadequate, exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and alternative dimensionality analyses will be performed. Psychometric evaluation will include internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), test-retest reliability (ICC(2,1)), ceiling/floor effects, and construct validity against Thai SF-36 and Thai FES-I. Planned comparisons include CFA two-factor versus empirically derived factor solutions and Rasch analysis. The main contribution is a validated Thai C19-YRSm with documented factor structure and measurement properties, enabling consistent assessment of long COVID severity in Thai clinical and research settings and informing cross-cultural instrument adaptation practices. Experiments: Dataset: Primary sample N=300–350 Thai adults aged ≥18 years with prior PCR/antigen-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection ≥4 weeks before enrolment and at least one persistent long-COVID symptom; pretest sample N=30. Instruments: Thai-translated C19-YRSm (all original items), Thai SF-36, Thai FES-I, Global Perceived Effect (GPE). Procedure: forward-back translation, expert committee review, cognitive pretesting (N=30), main administration (N≥300) with a 2-day retest for participants reporting GPE between -1 and 1. Baselines: (A) original two-factor C19-YRSm CFA model; (B) empirically derived EFA factor solution; (C) Rasch-calibrated model. Metrics: data suitability (KMO>0.6, Bartlett p<0.05), CFA fit indices (CFI≥0.95, TLI≥0.95, RMSEA≤0.06, SRMR≤0.08), EFA extraction (principal axis factoring, oblique rotation, eigenvalue>1), factor loadings (|loading|≥0.40), Cronbach's alpha per subscale ≥0.70 and ≤0.95, ICC(2,1) ≥0.75 for test-retest, floor/ceiling rates ≤15%, convergent validity correlations with SF-36 domains (expect |r|≥0.50 for related constructs), discriminant validity with FES-I (expect |r|≤0.30 where constructs differ). Statistical tests: Pearson or Spearman correlations based on normality (Kolmogorov-Smirnov), bootstrap 95% CIs for alphas and ICCs, significance α=0.05. Comparisons/Ablations: 1) CFA two-factor vs EFA three-factor vs Rasch: compare fit, reliability, and construct validity; 2) item ablation: remove ambiguous items (fatigue, cognition, post-exertional malaise) to evaluate change in model fit and Cronbach's alpha; 3) subgroup analyses by vaccination status, time since infection (<6 months vs ≥6 months), and recruitment setting (online vs clinic). Software: SPSS (EFA, reliability), IBM AMOS or equivalent (CFA), R or Winsteps for Rasch analysis. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sampling bias from convenience recruitment and overrepresentation of certain demographics (e.g., women, urban residents) limiting generalizability; heterogeneity in SARS-CoV-2 variants and time since infection confounding symptom patterns and dimensionality; reliance on self-report instruments introduces recall and reporting bias; short (2-day) retest interval may inflate ICCs due to recall but longer interval risks clinical change; item comprehension differences across education levels could distort factor structure; limited assessment of responsiveness to clinical change is not addressed by cross-sectional psychometrics; potential overfitting in EFA with sample-specific factor solutions; ceiling or floor effects may emerge in subpopulations and reduce discriminative capacity; computational/model risks include mis-specified CFA models, non-normal item distributions affecting fit indices, and insufficient subgroup sample sizes for planned comparisons.
